summary: Sedating first-generation antihistamine used short-term as an over-the-counter sleep aid. Strong anticholinergic effects and next-day sedation, especially in older adults.
description: Doxylamine is an over-the-counter antihistamine that makes people sleepy and is marketed as a short-term sleep aid. It can help with trouble falling or staying asleep but often causes dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, and next-day grogginess. It is strongly anticholinergic and appears on the Beers list, so it should generally be avoided in older adults and used cautiously in anyone with glaucoma, prostate issues, or urinary retention. It’s meant to be a temporary bridge, not a long-term insomnia solution.
patient_summary: Doxylamine is an OTC “nighttime” antihistamine that can make you sleepy. It may help for a few nights of bad insomnia but often leaves people feeling groggy or foggy the next day. It also dries things out—mouth, eyes, bowels—and can make peeing harder, especially if you have a large prostate. It’s usually not a good choice for people over 65.

primary.context: Used as an OTC short-term hypnotic for difficulty falling or staying asleep; not preferred for chronic insomnia due to anticholinergic side effects and tolerance.

off_label.context: Used off-label with pyridoxine for pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting when symptoms persist despite nonpharmacologic strategies and pyridoxine alone.

therapeutic_response.display: Sedation typically begins within 30–60 minutes after an oral dose.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Expect to feel sleepy at bedtime and possibly groggy the next morning. Avoid driving or tasks requiring full alertness until you know how it affects you.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Anticholinergic Effects (Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Dry mouth, trouble peeing, and constipation are frequent and can be more severe in older adults or when combined with other anticholinergic medications.
You may feel lightheaded when standing. Get up slowly to reduce fall risk.
Blurry vision can make reading and driving more difficult. Avoid night driving until you know your response.

serious_risks.risk: Severe confusion, delirium, or hallucinations (especially in older adults).
Urinary retention with painful or minimal urination.
Falls and fractures due to dizziness and sedation.
Paradoxical agitation, especially in children or at higher doses.
Worsening of sleep apnea or breathing problems when combined with other sedatives.

contraindications.contraindication: Concomitant use with other products containing doxylamine (OTC labeling)
Use when there is not enough time for a full night’s sleep (OTC labeling)
Hypersensitivity to doxylamine or any component (Canadian labeling)
Stenosing peptic ulcer or pyloroduodenal obstruction (Canadian labeling)
Concurrent use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (Canadian labeling)

precautions: CNS depression: May impair mental alertness and physical coordination; caution with driving and operating machinery.
Anticholinergic burden: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, and cognitive slowing are common.
Older adults: Beers Criteria identify doxylamine as potentially inappropriate due to anticholinergic toxicity and fall risk.
Paradoxical excitation: Some children and sensitive adults may become more agitated or restless instead of sleepy.
Respiratory conditions: Use caution in patients with apnea or chronic respiratory disease due to additive sedative effects with other CNS depressants.

interactions.interactant: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, and other CNS depressants
interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression, confusion, falls, and respiratory suppression.
interactions.action: Avoid combining when possible. If combination cannot be avoided, use the lowest doses and monitor closely for excessive sedation and breathing problems.

interactions.interactant: Other anticholinergic drugs (eg, tricyclics, antipsychotics, bladder antispasmodics)
interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of constipation, urinary retention, blurry vision, confusion, and delirium.
interactions.action: Review the total anticholinergic burden and minimize overlap, especially in older adults.

interactions.interactant: Other sedating antihistamines and OTC “PM” products
interactions.mechanism: Duplication of therapy, overdose risk, and marked sedation.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking OTC sleep aids. Check labels for doxylamine or diphenhydramine.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Sedation and next-day impairment: Assess morning grogginess, driving safety, and work/school performance.
Anticholinergic burden: Monitor for dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and cognitive changes, especially when combined with other anticholinergic medications.
Falls and balance: Ask older adults about dizziness, near-falls, and actual falls, particularly at night.
Sleep outcomes: Track sleep onset latency, total sleep time, and nocturnal awakenings to determine whether benefits outweigh side effects.
Paradoxical reactions: Watch for agitation, irritability, or insomnia worsening, especially in children and adolescents.
Overall medication list: Periodically review total sedative and anticholinergic load, particularly in patients with polypharmacy.

special_populations.pregnancy: In combination with pyridoxine, doxylamine is commonly used for pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting and has not been shown to increase baseline risk of major birth defects. For insomnia in pregnancy, behavioral approaches and safer pharmacologic options are generally preferred—discuss with OB and psychiatry.
special_populations.lactation: Doxylamine is expected to appear in breast milk. Infants may experience irritability, unusual sleepiness, or feeding difficulties. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time if needed and monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, or breathing concerns.
special_populations.pediatric: Insomnia: 25 mg PO once nightly for ages ≥12 years when recommended by a health care professional. Do not use in children <12 years for sleep. Children are more prone to paradoxical excitation.
special_populations.geriatric: Beers Criteria recommend avoiding doxylamine in adults ≥65 years due to strong anticholinergic effects, reduced clearance, and increased risk of confusion, falls, and dementia. Consider non-drug treatments and safer alternatives.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Excreted in urine as parent drug and metabolites; use caution in severe renal impairment and monitor for prolonged sedation.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No dose adjustment recommendations in labeling; consider starting cautiously in hepatic impairment.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally with measurable sedative effects within a few hours.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: 10–12 hours in adults; may be prolonged in older adults.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic metabolism via N-dealkylation to multiple metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Renal excretion of parent drug (~60%) and metabolites.

dosing.titration: Use the lowest effective dose, taken before bedtime, and limit duration to short-term use. This is a sedating medication—build in enough time for a full night’s sleep.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Doxylamine is not associated with classic physiologic dependence like benzodiazepines, but rebound insomnia and disrupted sleep can occur after regular use.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Doxylamine is an over-the-counter sedating antihistamine used short-term for insomnia. It is meant to be a temporary tool for trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, not a long-term fix.
items: Insomnia, sleep onset: Trouble falling asleep at bedtime.
Insomnia, sleep maintenance: Waking frequently and having difficulty returning to sleep.
Occasional short-term sleep disruption, often in the setting of stress or schedule changes.
off_label: Pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting when combined with pyridoxine, typically after non-drug strategies and pyridoxine alone are not enough.

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: I felt very sleepy within an hour and fell asleep faster than usual.
It knocked me out pretty hard, even at a single 25 mg dose.
I woke up feeling hungover and foggy the next morning.
I slept, but I was slow and out of it at work the following day.
items.note: Long half-life (10–12 hours) means sedation can carry over into daytime.

quotes: My mouth was so dry I had to keep water by the bed.
I felt constipated and a little blurry-eyed after a few nights.
items.note: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and blurry vision are common.

quotes: Instead of sleepy, I felt wired and restless.
My child got more irritable and hyper instead of sedated.
items.note: First-generation antihistamines can occasionally cause paradoxical agitation, especially in children.

sections.intro: People taking doxylamine for sleep usually notice strong sedation, but they also often describe classic anticholinergic effects.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Doxylamine has a relatively slow peak but a long half-life, so it can help with sleep but also lingers into the next day.
key_points: 30–60 minutes: Sedating effects begin; take ~30 minutes before bedtime.
2–4 hours: Peak blood levels and peak sedation.
10–12 hours: Average elimination half-life—sedation may persist into the morning, especially in older adults or at higher doses.
Prolonged in older adults: Clearance slows with age, increasing risk of confusion and falls.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Doxylamine can shorten sleep latency and reduce nighttime awakenings in the short term. However, tolerance to the sedating effects can develop, and side effects—particularly next-day grogginess and anticholinergic symptoms—limit its usefulness as a chronic sleep aid.
sections.metric: Subjective improvement in sleep onset and maintenance
sections.clinical_details: Evidence for long-term benefit in chronic insomnia is limited. Clinical guidelines generally recommend behavioral treatments and non-sedating options before sedating antihistamines. In older adults, the risks of falls, confusion, and anticholinergic burden usually outweigh the modest sleep benefits.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Strong anticholinergic and sedating effects increase risk of confusion, falls, urinary retention, and next-day impairment—especially in older adults.
other: CNS depression: May impair mental alertness and physical coordination; caution with driving and operating machinery.
Anticholinergic burden: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, and cognitive slowing are common.
Older adults: Beers Criteria identify doxylamine as potentially inappropriate due to anticholinergic toxicity and fall risk.
Paradoxical excitation: Some children and sensitive adults may become more agitated or restless instead of sleepy.
Respiratory conditions: Use caution in patients with apnea or chronic respiratory disease due to additive sedative effects with other CNS depressants.
patient_counseling: Do not use longer than 2 weeks for self-treated insomnia without talking to a clinician.
Avoid alcohol, other sleep aids, and sedating antihistamines while taking doxylamine.
If you are over 65, talk with your prescriber—safer alternatives are usually preferred.
Seek medical help right away if you have trouble urinating, severe confusion, chest pain, or breathing problems.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Sedation and anticholinergic effects dominate the side effect profile. Older adults are especially vulnerable to confusion and falls.
plain_language_list: Dizziness or feeling off-balance, especially when standing up.
Dry mouth, dry eyes, and thickened mucus.
Difficulty urinating, particularly in people with enlarged prostates.
Occasional paradoxical agitation or restlessness, especially in children.

sections.intro: Doxylamine adds to the effects of other sedating and anticholinergic medications. Polypharmacy is a major concern in older adults.

sections.heading: Stopping Safely
sections.text: Doxylamine is not associated with classic physiologic dependence like benzodiazepines, but rebound insomnia and disrupted sleep can occur after regular use.
key_points: Short-term use (a few nights): Can usually be stopped abruptly without medical issues, though sleep may feel lighter for a night or two.
Longer use (weeks): Some people notice rebound insomnia or vivid dreams when stopping.
Taper strategy: If used nightly for several weeks or longer, consider taking it every other night for a week, then a few nights per week before stopping completely.
Behavioral support: Pair discontinuation with sleep hygiene, regular wake times, and cognitive-behavioral strategies for insomnia when possible.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Use the lowest effective dose, taken before bedtime, and limit duration to short-term use. This is a sedating medication—build in enough time for a full night’s sleep.

adult.prn_use: Insomnia (sleep onset or maintenance): 25 mg PO once nightly, 30 minutes before bedtime, as needed for short-term use (generally ≤4–8 weeks).

sections.elderly: Avoid use in adults ≥65 years due to anticholinergic toxicity, confusion, and fall risk (Beers Criteria). If absolutely necessary, use the smallest possible dose with close monitoring and for the shortest duration.
sections.hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment provided in labeling.
sections.renal: No specific dosage adjustment provided, but ~60% of unchanged drug is excreted renally; use caution in severe impairment.
sections.simple_explanation: Take one tablet about half an hour before bed when you can get a full night of sleep. It stays in your system for many hours, so you may feel sleepy the next morning—especially if you are older or take other sedatives.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Use varies depending on age and indication. For insomnia, non-drug options are preferred whenever possible, particularly in pregnancy and older adults.
sections.pregnancy: In combination with pyridoxine, doxylamine is commonly used for pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting and has not been shown to increase baseline risk of major birth defects. For insomnia in pregnancy, behavioral approaches and safer pharmacologic options are generally preferred—discuss with OB and psychiatry.

sections.geriatrics: Beers Criteria recommend avoiding doxylamine in adults ≥65 years due to strong anticholinergic effects, reduced clearance, and increased risk of confusion, falls, and dementia. Consider non-drug treatments and safer alternatives.
sections.hepatic: No dose adjustment recommendations in labeling; consider starting cautiously in hepatic impairment.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation and next-day impairment: Assess morning grogginess, driving safety, and work/school performance.
Anticholinergic burden: Monitor for dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, and cognitive changes, especially when combined with other anticholinergic medications.
Falls and balance: Ask older adults about dizziness, near-falls, and actual falls, particularly at night.
Sleep outcomes: Track sleep onset latency, total sleep time, and nocturnal awakenings to determine whether benefits outweigh side effects.
Paradoxical reactions: Watch for agitation, irritability, or insomnia worsening, especially in children and adolescents.
Overall medication list: Periodically review total sedative and anticholinergic load, particularly in patients with polypharmacy.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Multiple OTC formulations exist; strengths and inactive ingredients can vary by brand.
items: Tablet, oral, as succinate: 25 mg (eg, FT Sleep Aid and generic equivalents).
Other OTC branded and store-brand doxylamine 25 mg tablets or capsules may be available.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Doxylamine competitively blocks histamine H1 receptors and also has central anticholinergic activity. By dampening histamine signaling and depressing vestibular and labyrinthine function, it produces sedation and anti-nausea effects.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: As a sedating first-generation antihistamine, doxylamine is considered a short-term, symptomatic option for insomnia rather than a core treatment. For chronic insomnia, behavioral approaches (CBT-I), circadian work, and safer pharmacologic options are preferred. In older adults, it is generally avoided due to anticholinergic toxicity and fall risk.

faqs.a: Doxylamine is an over-the-counter sedating antihistamine most often used short-term to help with insomnia—difficulty falling or staying asleep. It is also used, in combination with pyridoxine, for pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting. It is not recommended for long-term insomnia treatment.

faqs.q: How do I take doxylamine for sleep?
faqs.a: For adults, a common dose is 25 mg by mouth once nightly, about 30 minutes before bedtime, when you have enough time for a full night of sleep. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time, and avoid combining it with other sedatives or alcohol.

faqs.q: How long does doxylamine stay in your system?
faqs.a: Doxylamine has a half-life of about 10–12 hours. That means the sedating effects can carry into the next morning, especially in older adults or those with kidney problems. You may feel groggy or slowed the day after taking it.

faqs.q: Is doxylamine safe for older adults?
faqs.a: In general, no. Doxylamine is on the Beers list of medications to avoid in adults 65 and older because of strong anticholinergic effects and increased risk of confusion, falls, constipation, and urinary retention. Safer alternatives and non-medication sleep strategies are preferred.

faqs.q: Can I take doxylamine while pregnant?
faqs.a: Doxylamine combined with pyridoxine is commonly used for pregnancy-associated nausea and vomiting and has not been shown to increase the baseline risk of major birth defects. For insomnia in pregnancy, non-drug approaches and other options are typically considered first. Always discuss with your obstetric and mental health providers before using any sleep medicine in pregnancy.

Doxylamine does not cause classic dependence like benzodiazepines, but people can become psychologically reliant on it for sleep. With regular use, tolerance to the sedating effects can develop, and stopping may temporarily worsen insomnia. It’s best used short-term while addressing the root causes of sleep problems.

faqs.q: Can I use doxylamine for my child’s sleep?
faqs.a: Doxylamine should not be used for insomnia in children under 12 years without medical guidance. In younger children, sedating antihistamines can cause paradoxical agitation and are not considered safe or appropriate routine sleep aids.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with doxylamine?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol adds to the sedative effects of doxylamine and increases the risk of dangerous drowsiness, poor judgment, accidents, and breathing problems. Avoid alcohol when using any sedating sleep medicine.
